newsitem.title: UK: UK economy in good shape despite export woes - CBI.
newsitem.headline: UK economy in good shape despite export woes - CBI.

text.p: The outlook for the British economy is good and should remain so if the new Labour government keeps its economic promises, the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said on Monday.
CBI director-general Adair Turner said times were tough for exporters because of the pound's strength, but a strong currency reflected international confidence in the British economy.

"Our new government's economic inheritance is a fairly good one," Turner told the CBI West Midlands' summer banquet in Birmingham. "We have low and stable inflation and public finances coming under control."

He said British business was better equipped to succeed on the world market than for many years. "Tough though it may be for exporting companies, one of the reasons sterling is so high is international confidence in the British economy's underlying strength."
The pound has rocketed by about 25 percent on a trade-weighted basis, in a little less than a year.
Turner said the first two months of the new Labour administration showed the government had no intention of unravelling the market liberalisation that had taken place over the past 15 years.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget had demonstrated a clear commitment to sound public finances as well as a "New Labour" approach to tax and spending. But Turner said more should have been to dampen domestic demand.
"Nobody should believe there's a magic wand which will control the exchange rate, nor pretend that monetary policy won't play a key role in controlling inflationary pressures.

"But we do feel that the Chancellor missed an opportunity to at least offset a bit of the imbalance within our economy -- between a very buoyant consumer sector and our hard-pressed exporters," he said.

Both the July budget and previous chancellor Kenneth Clarke's last one in November had been too slack on the consumer side and the new government might have to grasp the nettle far more tightly next year, he said.

The tight public spending plans laid down by the government also represented a huge challenge, Turner said. "The government will need to consider radical approaches in many areas -- health, welfare, education and transport -- if it is to succeed."
Noting that Britain had signed up to the European Union's Social Chapter, which guarantees minimum employment rights, Turner said:

"The challenge now is to ensure that it doesn't become the mechanism for spreading bad rather than good practice across Europe. So far, the Prime Minister has lived up to his promise to campaign in Europe for flexible approaches -- it is an argument that has to be won."
